newsitem.title: UK: Hague to rally Scots Tories after election blow.
newsitem.headline: Hague to rally Scots Tories after election blow.

text.p: FILED AS AN OVERNIGHTER
By James Forrester

PERTH, Scotland, June 27 (REUTER) - Britain's new Conservative leader William Hague makes his first public appeal to rank-and-file members on Friday with a rallying call to a Scottish party stunned by a general election wipeout and riven by internal dissent.

Hague winds up the annual Scottish Conservative conference amid dispute over its stance on the referendum for a separate Scottish parliament, planned for Autumn by the new Labour government, and the reason for failure in the May 1 election.

Opposition to any change in the 300-year-old link with England was a major factor in the party's disastrous election campaign. Hague reiterated that opposition on a fleeting visit to Glasgow and Edinburgh last Saturday.

Former cabinet minister Peter Lilley gave the same message at a private pre-conference meeting on Thursday. He stressed, however, that Conservative policies must have "a Scottish dimension tailored to the needs, opportunities and hopes of the Scottish people".
Lilley said Conservative policies had restored the economy and Labour only became electable by adopting them wholesale.
Many Scots party activists regard a devolved parliament as inevitable and say Conservatives should work for maximum representation in it.

Opinion polls since the May 1 general election -- when Conservatives lost all 10 Scottish seats held in the old parliament -- show the majority of Scots want their own parliament and at least 25 percent of Conservatives are in favour.
Some grass-roots workers attribute the election failure that virtually wiped them off the political map in Scotland to a perception of the party as English-dominated.

This was reinforced by Hague's victory in the leadership election. Scots had no vote in the contest as they had no M.Ps. but soundings at all party levels overwhelmingly favoured former Chancellor Kenneth Clark.
Several pro-devolution members are in effect boycotting the Perth conference.
"I refuse to give blind homage to a leader whom I did not have any part in electing," said Brian Meek.
"I know little of his policies other than his distaste for devolution and his suspicions about Europe.
"Neither of these brought us rip-roaring success."
Meek, chairman of the Conservative group on Edinburgh city council, is one of only 82 Conservatives among the 1245 local councillors in Scotland.

He claims the one-day conference -- a far cry from the rousing two- or three-day events used by former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher to launch her most adventurous policies -- has been "stitched-up" by the present leadership. Meek is attending the Wimbledon tennis championships instead.
Other activists suggest Conservatives will only regain support by forming a separate Scottish party that elects its own leadership free of control by Central Office in London.
The party, bereft of MPs and without any European MPs, has little electoral base left in Scotland.
It failed to win control of any local authorities in the 1995 council elections.

It has no voice in parliament's Scottish Grand Committee which considers legislation relating to Scotland, as only the 72 members for Scottish constituencies can take part. Hague has appointed three Scots elected by English constituencies to speak on Scottish affairs in the House of Commons.

Arthur Bell, chairman of the centre-left Scottish Conservative Reform Group, has been castigated by party chairman Annabel Goldie and president David McLetchie for getting funds from the Konrad Adenauer Foundation to study devolution in Germany and the relationship between the pan-German CDU party and its CSU partner in Bavaria.
